Gnädigster Herr
Mein erſter Vorſaz war, Ewr Hochfürſtl. Durchlaucht durchaus keine Audiosa mehr
zu melden, und Dinge die nicht mehr zu andern wären ihren Gang gehen zu laßen.
Nothgedrungen aber muß ich diesen Vorsazz aufgeben und Hochstderoselbe Hülfe recta
mirn — die Sache ist diese.
Ehe ich hieher gieng erhielt ich das Lub Lili A beigebogene Schreiben des v. Bornstadt
in Posen. Ich hätte von dem Verfaßer keine gute Meinung und suchte ihm dadurch
zu demüthigen, daß ich dh. p. Glenck ein bloßes Recipisse geben lies, da es in Sachen
Sr Durch ein Schreiben d. po Bomstadt eingegangen wäre, worüber er als General
Mandatarius ihm bescheiden würde.
Ich suchte u Person als dann noch den Melzer und den Pre: Braunschuſung zu gewinnen
ein alles aufzubieten, daß die Berliner Verfügung aufrecht erhalten und die
Gelder deponirt werden mögten beſonders aber daß Broniewski gleich exmittirt
werden mögte. Mann versprach mir dies und ich reisete allen in der Nacht
hierher nach Betsche, ſchickte ſogleich einen reitenden Boten nach Franckfurth
und beſtellte Meyer Bernhard und Conſorten hier her. Beigehende Abſchrift
Lub B beſagt das weitere.
Nach dieser Expedition bis ich die Deputirten welche in Breslau waren rußen
äußerst befremdend war es mich daß keiner erscheinen wolte, endlich er
fuhr ich daß die Leute aufgehögt waren vom Kauf zurückzutreten,
Ich suchte den Grund zu erforschen, und höhrte zu meinen Schrecken, daß der Rochlitz
die Leute die Köpfe verwirre und ſie drohe, alles zu zerreißen, weil er um
sein Schwager Klein einen Contract in Händen hätte nach welchen sie das Vor-

Vorwerk Abre und den grösten Theil der Waldung abnehmen würden.
Der Justiz Burge Meister Metzig, der als Beistand der Gemeinde ernannt
ist, erklärte mir endlich gerade hin, daß ihm H. B. v. Glenck angelegen die
ganze Verhandlung in Breslau zu zureichten, daß er große Forderung
habe die er geltend machen würde, und daß er Henck, wenn er der
Metzig mit ihm halten wolle, sehr erkenntlich sein würde.
Er Metzig erklärte ferner, daß er zwar sehe daß man Ewr Durchlau¬
prellen wolle, daß er aber als Beistand der Gemeinden darauf bei
stehen müße.

Schreiben des v. Bornstädt, erfuhr auch noch von mehreren Einsaßen daß

zu zernichten, er wolte ſie alle davor glücklich machen
Warum Glenck dies thut bleibt im Rathsel.
Ich erwartete übrigens seine und Wunsters Ankunft-Glenck erfolgte vor
gestern. Ich war bemüht alles auf das gelindeste zu erforschen habe aber
nichts weiter von ihm heraus gebracht, daß er nichts wiße indem
ihm die Pappiere mangelten, auf die Frage wo der zwischen ihm und
dem Leixner geschloßene Contract sey, antwortet er, daß solchen
der Lieut: v Brandenstein hinter sich habe, und auf sein Gut oder das
Geld dafür dringen würde.

beigehendes Schreiben des v Bornstädt sub d aber beweis daß Glenck mir belogen und
daß der Contract bereits an, Kaufmann Klein einen Vetter des Röcklis
Cedirt sey. Noch zweifelte ich und suchte alles mit den Leuten aufs Beste
zu arangiren, bis ich beigehendes Billet sub C von Meyer Bernhard
erhielt. Dies veranlaßt mich diese Estaffette schleunig an Ewr Durchlaucht
zu senden.
Sowohl die Gemeinden, als die Franckfartler bestehen darauf daß dieser
zwischen Leixner und den Herrn v. Brandenstein geschloßene Contract
vor allen Dingen herbey geſchaft, um völlig Cassirt werde.

tract heraus giebt.

Extaffitte ſchreiben daß er ſofort dieſe ſamtl Pappiere heraus giebt, und
daß so wohl er als Herr v Brandenstein ſich wegen der Aufhebung beide
Contracte gerichtl. reverirn, daß sie weiter nichts von die Franckfurther
herren, — oder von die Betecher Gründe praetendiren können, oder mögen.
v Brandenstein, der schwerlich von alle die Drehereien des H. Glenck was wißen
mag, wird den Reversch dorten gewis gleich ausſtellen, und ich bitte unterthänig
daß Ewr Durchlaucht diesen jungen Mann, der wohl an der Sache ganz unsthuldig

sein mag, höchst Ihre Gnade nicht zu entziehen. Ich werde auch dafür in meinen Erster
nicht ermüden.

Ja auf das eiligste zur Estaffette hier her zu senden. Den sonsten kan ich nichts
mit den Leuten abmachen.

Zurück schaft um selbigen nebst den Locietrets Contract zurük giebt und

Ich hätte Ewer Durchl. gerne mit dieser Sache verschont. Ich komme aber anders
nicht durch, den die Leute bestehen darauf.
Mit Bomstadt sieht alles schrecklich verworren aus Glenck Rochlitz [Werleben?]
Bornſtädt, und wie das Gesindel alles heißt, haben ſich ſtets wie die
Keßelflicker unter Ewr Durchlaucht Augen gezänckt, im Grunde
aber haben sie alle in brüderlicher Eintracht betrogen, daß jedem die
Haare zu Berge stehen. Ewr Durchlaucht wäre es stets den sie alle
gerne reine ausgeplündert hätte.
Der Wald ist ganz ruinirt und was die Diebe noch ein Jahrhier ge¬
Laußet hätte, so waren die ſchönen Güter nicht 50000 mehr werth –
Jezt bin ich bemüht den Bornstädt so recht solide zu überflügeln.
Er ſchien Gebrauch von den Verkauf am der Unterthanen zu machen.

gemachter Sache ſezzen laßen. Da werde ich den wohl mit den Helden
fertig werden – Schändlich ist es mir daß solche infamun in dem
Acten vorkommen, so sagt der Bornstadt zu Beispiel Bey

anderer Pächter verſprach ihn nach Jahres Frist mehr darum wolte er
mich vertreiben, um wieder 600 Rthl zu erpreßen.
Unwahr, sagt er weiter, muß er doch wohl sein, daß der Herr
Fürst, wie Glenck sich rühmt, um solche Prelliren weis¬
den der Fürst hatt doch den Auf des erhabensten grösten Mannes und Men¬
sehen freundes
Rasend mögte ich werden wenn ich so was vor Augen bekomme, und
ich kan weiter nichts wünschen als alle diese schmuggige Dinge zu beseitigen
und dergestalt aus der Welt zu ſchaffen, daß Ewr Durchlaucht keinen Ver
dens mehr haben.

Bornstädt, wan er Betschen für 200000 Rthl verkaufen hilft, 1000 stück
frid: Sor zugesagt. Glenck hat dies hier vor dem Metzig bestätiget.

ihm abfinden? Geruhen Sie gnädigster Fürst mir desfals eine
Weisung zu gebe.
Die Pacht Sache würde ich rechtens abmachen, und bey Gott nichts ver¬
ſchneben, aber in der Geſchichte kan ich ohne Ewr Durchl. Befehl nichts
weiter thun. Generals, um Gott weis welche Menschen alle in

translation.en: Most Serene Prince, Most gracious Lord! My first resolve was to report no further Odiosa whatever to Your Most Serene Highness, and to let things that could no longer be altered take their course. Compelled by necessity, however, I must abandon this resolve and [uncertain: recta mirn] Your Highness's own assistance — the matter is this. Before I went hither I received the letter of v. Bornstadt in Posen enclosed sub Lit. A. I had no good opinion of its author and sought to humble him by having a bare acknowledgement of receipt given him through Mr. Glenck, to the effect that a letter of Mr. Bomstadt had come in in His Serene Highness's affairs, upon which he, as General Mandatarius, would inform him. I then further sought to win over, in person, Melzer and the Pre: [uncertain: Braunschuſung], and to muster everything so that the Berlin disposition might be upheld and the monies deposited, but above all that Broniewski might be evicted at once. This was promised me, and I travelled off in the night hither to Betsche, at once sent a mounted messenger to Franckfurth, and summoned Meyer Bernhard and consorts hither. The enclosed Copy, sub B, states the rest. After this expedition I [uncertain: called] the deputies who were in Breslau; it was exceedingly strange to me that none of them would appear; at length I learned that the people had been stirred up to withdraw from the purchase. I sought to discover the reason, and heard to my horror that Rochlitz was confusing the people's heads and threatening them, to tear everything up, because for his brother-in-law Klein he had a contract in his hands by which they would take over the

demesne farm [uncertain: Abre] and the greater part of the woodland. The justice-burgomaster Metzig, who is appointed as legal assistant to the commune, at length declared to me straight out that Mr. B. v. Glenck was concerned to arrange the whole negotiation in Breslau, that he had large claims which he would press, and that he, Glenck, would be very appreciative if he, Metzig, would side with him. He, Metzig, further declared that he indeed saw that Your Serene Highness was to be cheated, but that as legal assistant to the communes he must insist that, first, this matter be entirely settled, and secondly, that with Mr. v. Bornstädt everything must first be cleared away; sooner than that the communes can pay no money and can enter into nothing. After this sad experience I received the letter of v. Bornstädt enclosed as Lub c, and learned besides from several inhabitants that Mr. Glenck had requested them to withdraw from the contract and to annul it; he would make them all happy in return. Why Glenck does this remains a riddle. For the rest, I awaited his and Wunster's arrival — Glenck's took place the day before yesterday. I took pains to explore everything in the gentlest manner, but got nothing further out of him than that he knows nothing, since the papers were wanting to him; to the question where the contract concluded between him and Leixner might be, he answers that Lieut. v. Brandenstein has it in his keeping, and would press for his estate or the money for it.

The enclosed letter of v. Bornstädt sub d, however, proves that Glenck lied to me and that the contract has already been ceded to the merchant Klein, a cousin of Rochlitz. I still doubted, and sought to arrange everything with the people for the best, until I received the enclosed note sub C from Meyer Bernhard. This moves me to send this express courier in haste to Your Serene Highness. Both the communes and the Frankfurt men insist that this contract concluded between Leixner and Mr. v. Brandenstein be, before all else, brought forth and completely cancelled. Secondly, Bernhard and Leixner will pay not a Groschen further until Glenck surrenders the partnership contract concluded between them. Thirdly, the communes insist that everything be settled with Bornstädt; sooner than that they will agree to nothing further. My counsel and petition is this: that Your Most Serene Highness write to Glenck by express courier that he surrender all these papers at once, and that both he and Mr. v. Brandenstein enter judicial written undertakings as to the cancellation of both contracts, so that they can or may claim nothing further from the Frankfurt gentlemen — or from the Betsche lands. V. Brandenstein, who can hardly know anything of all Mr. Glenck's twistings, will certainly issue the written undertaking there at once, and I petition most humbly that Your Serene Highness not withdraw your grace from this young man, who may well be entirely innocent

in the matter. Nor shall I tire in my [uncertain: efforts] on his behalf. May Your Most Serene Highness be pleased to send me the written undertaking from Mr. v. Brandenstein hither with all speed by express courier. For otherwise I can settle nothing with the people. But let Your Highness command Glenck that he here at once fetch back the ceded contract and surrender the same together with the partnership contract, and judicially renounce all claims. I would gladly have spared Your Serene Highness this business. But I cannot get through otherwise, for the people insist upon it. With Bomstadt everything looks dreadfully tangled. Glenck, [uncertain: Kochlitz/Rochlitz], [uncertain: Werleben], Bornstädt, and whatever all the rabble are called, have constantly quarrelled like tinkers before Your Serene Highness's eyes, but at bottom they have all cheated in brotherly concord, so that anyone's hair would stand on end. It was always Your Serene Highness whom they would all gladly have plundered clean. The forest is entirely ruined, and had the thieves gone on [uncertain: cutting] here another year, the fine estates would no longer have been worth 50000 — Now I am at pains to outflank Bornstädt really soundly. He seemed to intend to make use of the sale to the subjects; but these I have brought so far that they leave him, against my guarantee, until the matter is concluded. Then I shall doubtless get the better of the hero — It is shameful to me that such infamies occur in the files; thus Bornstadt says, for example: at the

commencement of my lease I had to lay out 500 Rthl to Glenck as proxenticium; another tenant promised him more after a year's term, and therefore he wished to drive me out, in order to extort another 600 Rthl. It must indeed be untrue, he goes on to say, that the Prince, as Glenck boasts, knows of such cheating, for the Prince has the repute of the most exalted, greatest of men and friend of mankind. I could go mad when such a thing comes before my eyes, and I can wish nothing further than to clear away all these grubby things and to be rid of them so utterly that Your Serene Highness may have no further [uncertain: vexation]. What torments me most at present is this — Your Serene Highness has promised Bornstädt 1000 pieces of Fried:d'or if he helps sell Betschen for 200000 Rthl. Glenck has confirmed this here before Metzig. What am I, a poor man, now to answer to that? The fellow tenders in this regard the oath to Your Serene Highness, to Glenck, and to Rochlitz. What am I to answer the fellow on this, and with what am I to satisfy him? Be pleased, most gracious Prince, to give me an instruction in this regard. The lease matter I would settle at law, and by God cut nothing short, but in this history I can do nothing further without Your Serene Highness's command. Generals, and God knows what people, all take an interest on behalf of the poor wretch and his wife, who seems to be a real Xantippe

to be; therefore I wish to be rid of the wretched B. in a decent manner. As regards the timber contracts, matters look just as ugly — for so far as they exist, they belonged to Rochlitz under other names — and the name-bearers now all cry out that they want no money but the quantities of timber specified in the contracts. This is now to be another motive for annulling the purchase with the subjects. But here I shall speak loudly with the [uncertain: patrons]. For the whole commune will come forward and loudly prove the villains' infamies — Your Serene Highness will be astonished at all these knaveries. This very moment I learn of a new intrigue of Glenck's — I had, as said before, brought Meyer Bernhard so far that he meant to be in Posen on the evening of the 29th or early on the 30th with the 66000 Rthl. At this moment Wünster tells me that Glenck has talked Meyer Bernhard into not paying the money on the 29th but going to Breslau and asking Your Serene Highness what he should do — for it would not be necessary before the 2nd of August that the money be lodged with Broniewski. The Jew now twists again, says he would do it, since he has so many claims upon Your Serene Highness. We all sit here now like fools — It is more than too bad.

what these people permit themselves — As regards the Kaemener and Kulmner dismemberment I can likewise do nothing for the present. For Glenck has already betrayed everything to him (of which the enclosed letter Lub f is the proof), everything, in order to earn something. O God! what shameful people are these? I shall see what the Jew will do; if he insists on the journey to Breslau, then I shall only see how I can get half-way finished with the subjects here, and shall come there too at that time; but then I petition Your Serene Highness also, most heartily, to work over all these B: really roughly, so that they may at last be brought to fear and may cease their damned menées. In deepest reverence I remain, until death, Your Most Serene Highness's [most humble servant]. May Your Most Serene Highness be pleased to send the express courier with all the papers to Posen, to old Reinhardt. If I can still turn everything, I shall be there — if not, then he must send them to me hither. Ah, it is now a true torment of hell to bring these people to reason. The letter to my daughter I most submissively beg to have delivered, and if anything has come in there from South Prussia etc., to let it go with the express courier to me. Betsch, the 26th of July 1804, faithful humble and obedient servant, v Triebenfeld

Why Glenck does this remains a riddle. For the rest, I awaited his and Wunster's arrival — Glenck's took place the day before yesterday. I took pains to explore everything in the gentlest manner, but got nothing further out of him than that he knows nothing, since the papers were wanting to him; to the question where the contract concluded between him and Leixner might be, he answers that Lieut. v. Brandenstein has it in his keeping, and would press for his estate or the money for it.

The enclosed letter of v. Bornstädt sub d, however, proves that Glenck lied to me and that the contract has already been ceded to the merchant Klein, a cousin of Rochlitz. I still doubted, and sought to arrange everything with the people for the best, until I received the enclosed note sub C from Meyer Bernhard. This moves me to send this express courier in haste to Your Serene Highness. Both the communes and the Frankfurt men insist that this contract concluded between Leixner and Mr. v. Brandenstein be, before all else, brought forth and completely cancelled. Secondly, Bernhard and Leixner will pay not a Groschen further until Glenck surrenders the partnership contract concluded between them. Thirdly, the communes insist that everything be settled with Bornstädt; sooner than that they will agree to nothing further. My counsel and petition is this: that Your Most Serene Highness write to Glenck by express courier that he surrender all these papers at once, and that both he and Mr. v. Brandenstein enter judicial written undertakings as to the cancellation of both contracts, so that they can or may claim nothing further from the Frankfurt gentlemen — or from the Betsche lands. V. Brandenstein, who can hardly know anything of all Mr. Glenck's twistings, will certainly issue the written undertaking there at once, and I petition most humbly that Your Serene Highness not withdraw your grace from this young man, who may well be entirely innocent

in the matter. Nor shall I tire in my [uncertain: efforts] on his behalf. May Your Most Serene Highness be pleased to send me the written undertaking from Mr. v. Brandenstein hither with all speed by express courier. For otherwise I can settle nothing with the people. But let Your Highness command Glenck that he here at once fetch back the ceded contract and surrender the same together with the partnership contract, and judicially renounce all claims. I would gladly have spared Your Serene Highness this business. But I cannot get through otherwise, for the people insist upon it. With Bomstadt everything looks dreadfully tangled. Glenck, [uncertain: Kochlitz/Rochlitz], [uncertain: Werleben], Bornstädt, and whatever all the rabble are called, have constantly quarrelled like tinkers before Your Serene Highness's eyes, but at bottom they have all cheated in brotherly concord, so that anyone's hair would stand on end. It was always Your Serene Highness whom they would all gladly have plundered clean. The forest is entirely ruined, and had the thieves gone on [uncertain: cutting] here another year, the fine estates would no longer have been worth 50000 — Now I am at pains to outflank Bornstädt really soundly. He seemed to intend to make use of the sale to the subjects; but these I have brought so far that they leave him, against my guarantee, until the matter is concluded. Then I shall doubtless get the better of the hero — It is shameful to me that such infamies occur in the files; thus Bornstadt says, for example: at the

commencement of my lease I had to lay out 500 Rthl to Glenck as proxenticium; another tenant promised him more after a year's term, and therefore he wished to drive me out, in order to extort another 600 Rthl. It must indeed be untrue, he goes on to say, that the Prince, as Glenck boasts, knows of such cheating, for the Prince has the repute of the most exalted, greatest of men and friend of mankind. I could go mad when such a thing comes before my eyes, and I can wish nothing further than to clear away all these grubby things and to be rid of them so utterly that Your Serene Highness may have no further [uncertain: vexation]. What torments me most at present is this — Your Serene Highness has promised Bornstädt 1000 pieces of Fried:d'or if he helps sell Betschen for 200000 Rthl. Glenck has confirmed this here before Metzig. What am I, a poor man, now to answer to that? The fellow tenders in this regard the oath to Your Serene Highness, to Glenck, and to Rochlitz. What am I to answer the fellow on this, and with what am I to satisfy him? Be pleased, most gracious Prince, to give me an instruction in this regard. The lease matter I would settle at law, and by God cut nothing short, but in this history I can do nothing further without Your Serene Highness's command. Generals, and God knows what people, all take an interest on behalf of the poor wretch and his wife, who seems to be a real Xantippe

to be; therefore I wish to be rid of the wretched B. in a decent manner. As regards the timber contracts, matters look just as ugly — for so far as they exist, they belonged to Rochlitz under other names — and the name-bearers now all cry out that they want no money but the quantities of timber specified in the contracts. This is now to be another motive for annulling the purchase with the subjects. But here I shall speak loudly with the [uncertain: patrons]. For the whole commune will come forward and loudly prove the villains' infamies — Your Serene Highness will be astonished at all these knaveries. This very moment I learn of a new intrigue of Glenck's — I had, as said before, brought Meyer Bernhard so far that he meant to be in Posen on the evening of the 29th or early on the 30th with the 66000 Rthl. At this moment Wünster tells me that Glenck has talked Meyer Bernhard into not paying the money on the 29th but going to Breslau and asking Your Serene Highness what he should do — for it would not be necessary before the 2nd of August that the money be lodged with Broniewski. The Jew now twists again, says he would do it, since he has so many claims upon Your Serene Highness. We all sit here now like fools — It is more than too bad.

what these people permit themselves — As regards the Kaemener and Kulmner dismemberment I can likewise do nothing for the present. For Glenck has already betrayed everything to him (of which the enclosed letter Lub f is the proof), everything, in order to earn something. O God! what shameful people are these? I shall see what the Jew will do; if he insists on the journey to Breslau, then I shall only see how I can get half-way finished with the subjects here, and shall come there too at that time; but then I petition Your Serene Highness also, most heartily, to work over all these B: really roughly, so that they may at last be brought to fear and may cease their damned menées. In deepest reverence I remain, until death, Your Most Serene Highness's [most humble servant]. May Your Most Serene Highness be pleased to send the express courier with all the papers to Posen, to old Reinhardt. If I can still turn everything, I shall be there — if not, then he must send them to me hither. Ah, it is now a true torment of hell to bring these people to reason. The letter to my daughter I most submissively beg to have delivered, and if anything has come in there from South Prussia etc., to let it go with the express courier to me. Betsch, the 26th of July 1804, faithful humble and obedient servant, v Triebenfeld
summary_en: Reports the collapse of the Betsche sale to the peasant communes: Glenck is accused of urging the villagers to withdraw, of lying about the contract with Leixner (in fact ceded to the merchant Klein, cousin of Rochlitz), and of persuading Meyer Bernhard to delay paying 66000 Rthl at Posen. Encloses letters from v. Bornstädt (who claims a promised 1000 Friedrichsd'or for selling Betschen at 200000 Rthl and alleges a 500 Rthl proxenticium to Glenck), asks for express orders compelling Glenck and Lieut. v. Brandenstein to surrender and judicially cancel both contracts, and complains of ruined woodland and fraudulent timber contracts.
summary_de: Bericht über die gefährdete Veräußerung von Betsche: Glenck habe die Gemeinden zum Rücktritt vom Kaufvertrag aufgestachelt, den mit Leixner geschlossenen Contract über Klein, einen Verwandten des Rochlitz, cediert und leugne dies; Justizbürgermeister Metzig und v. Bornstädt (Beilagen A–F) bestätigten die Umtriebe. Gefordert werden fürstliche Befehle per Estafette an Glenck und Lieut. v. Brandenstein zur Herausgabe und gerichtlichen Cassation beider Contracte sowie des Societätsvertrags. Meyer Bernhard verzögere die Zahlung der 66000 Rthl in Posen; Bornstädt berufe sich auf zugesagte 1000 Fried:d'or bei Verkauf für 200000 Rthl; der Wald sei ruiniert.
